craft_claim: Reporting familiar or horrific material in stripped, procedural description de-automatizes perception and renews attention (ostranenie); empirical work links foregrounding to felt affect.

supporting_evidence.location: Opening and sections on Tolstoy's technique
supporting_evidence.note: Shklovsky argues perception is automatized by habit and that art removes objects from automatization, describing events as if for the first time without using the accepted names of their parts.
Foregrounded stylistic features predicted defamiliarization, which in turn evoked feeling, supporting the claim that stripped but selected description reactivates attention.

supporting_evidence.location: Partition and street narratives (e.g., the flat reporting of atrocity)
supporting_evidence.note: Manto reports communal violence through plain declaratives and concrete acts rather than commentary, renewing attention to the event by refusing its conventional emotional framing.

counterevidence.note: Section G failure G2: stripping is not sufficient, because where the plain surface carries no foregrounded selection the same foregrounding mechanism yields no affect and the passage reads as machine flatness; section B also labels the 'one charged detail' prediction a card exercise rather than a tested result.

scope: Description of violence, routine, and over-familiar material.
exceptions: Audiences already unfamiliar with the material gain nothing from estrangement and may need orientation instead.
